## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Linemen and line inspectors who patrol a utility's poles.
   [HN] "Most utilities solve this problem with foot patrols. Linemen drive out with a clipboard or an iPad, and run
   through a checklist with binoculars to visually confirm everything is in order." [HN] "We're making weatherized,
   hybrid-fixed drones deployed for power utility inspections." → `roles[lineman]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Confirm every pole and line is sound before it fails.
   [HN] "But when the wood starts to rot, or the cotter pin falls out, and a live conductor is dropped on a dead tree on
   a windy day, you get devastating wildfires like the Palisades Fire in LA last year." → `context.job`,
   `statements.problem`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** On an inspection patrol, pole by pole from the ground; and reactive patrols after storms or a
   strange feeder reading.
   [HN] "A lineman can inspect about 50-150 poles per day, yet even the smallest rural electric cooperatives (with about
   ~20 employees) have about 50,000 distribution poles. Clearly the math doesn't work out. As a result, a given utility
   pole is inspected about every 10 years". [HN] "If there's a weird harmonic on a feeder, or a utility needs a rapid
   scan after a storm, we can get on-site within minutes to inspect." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: pole
   inspection patrol`. Author's choice: the window {3, MONTHS} (the research's "monthly cycle" rhythm; spec 120 reads a
   monthly rhythm as 3 MONTHS), Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most": not every lineman is put
   on patrols in a quarter; storm and construction crews may not be).

4. **Which people.** Linemen and inspectors at US electric utilities and rural co-ops.
   [HN] "The U.S. has 7M miles of power lines (enough to go to the moon and back 14 times), and they're aging." [HN]
   "Power utilities are our first customers". → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The utility, per pole or tower inspected.
   [HN] "Our business model is straightforward: inspection as a service. We charge per pole or tower." [HN] "We just
   secured our first major contract and are working out the details of pilots with some big utilities. Our first paid
   flight is mid-April." [LYC1] "If you're interested in piloting our service, reach out to avi@voltairlabs.com" →
   `persona.decision_maker: {role: manager}`. Author's choice: the decider is the utility's inspection manager and the
   tested role "The VP of operations" (with "The co-op board" listed): no public source names a buyer title. Purchase
   friction's tested item "An FAA waiver to fly beyond sight" is from [HN] (avigotskind, a founder): "There's no real
   way around BVLOS regs right now. The real problem is BVLOS + need to recharge." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444564 ;
   the pad safety review is from [HN] "The risk of landing a drone multiple times per day at myriad points around the
   network felt too risky for utility engineers."; the competitive bid is the author's. Commitment's step "pay for a
   pilot on one feeder": [HN] "Our first paid flight is mid-April"; "on one feeder" is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Fixed-wing drones that live outside and recharge on pads along the lines.
   [HN] "We're making weatherized, long-range (well over 70 miles), fixed-wing drones that can live outside for months
   at a time. They recharge inductively (no connections or moving parts) on stripped-down charging pads that cost a
   couple thousand dollars apiece." [HN] "we use the charging station as an intermediary, dumping the data from our
   drone to a hard drive on the station over a high-speed WiFi link." [HN] (wweissbluth, a founder) "We're collecting
   61MP RGB, LiDAR (DSM DTM) and radiometric thermal for sensors" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444631 .
   The earlier idea, dropped before the HN post: [LYC1] "We build drones that charge directly on transmission lines."
   and [HN] "There's not enough current on distribution lines!" → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`.
   Compatibility (pole tops visible from above — tested; a spot for a pad; findings into the work order system) and
   Adoption friction (review the drone's flags before sending crews — tested; work from a defect list) are the
   author's, from the mechanism's needs. Relative advantage: [HN] "Xcel power found drones to find 60% more defects than
   foot patrols (because of pole-top vantage point)" (less_worry) and the 50-150 poles a day (shorter_time); wording the
   author's.

7. **Price and cost.**
   Price: **the operator's reading.** [HN] gives the unit only ("We charge per pole or tower"); no amount appears in any
   launch-era or later source. The founder's price is set at **$3 to $5 per pole, each**, below the author's estimate
   of the foot patrol's cost per pole, since the founders sell on cost ([HN] "Georgia Power saved 60% on operating
   expenses when they switched to using drones"). Under the engine's `compare` reading the founder's ratio is 30% to
   125% of the cost (CommercialChain.derive).
   Cost, MONEY **$4 to $10 of the pole inspections per pole, each**: author's arithmetic. A lineman's day of 8 hours at
   [BLS] "The median annual wage for electrical power-line installers and repairers was $95,320 in May 2025" ($45.83 an
   hour) is about $367; with a truck and fuel, about $500 a day; over [HN]'s 50-150 poles a day, $3.30 to $10 a pole,
   taken as $4 to $10. The helicopter ($25k a flight) and the drone-in-a-box ($250,000 a box) are left as the founders'
   comparisons in the statement, not folded into the per-pole cost.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (Uncle_Clark) "I work for a utility company and this is brilliant. One other issue that comes into play for
   inspections is right of way." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47446642 ; [HN] (lifis) "Why not just install
   cameras on the poles?" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47452396 ; [HN] (petargyurov, who builds analytics on
   drone and helicopter imagery) "This is a tough problem to solve and for a lot of operators ultimately comes down to
   cost." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444350 . No first-person lineman account exists in the sources.

## Status today

Widened in pitch, same buyer. [YCP] today reads "Autonomous Drones for Earth Observation", with power utilities "the
perfect first customer" ([LYC2] 2026-03-13: "Power utilities are the perfect first customer. ... Voltair can serve
existing multi-billion dollar data markets in road, rail and telecom inspection at 10x lower prices"). [SITE] still sells
utility inspection only ("Voltair | Autonomous Drone Inspection for Electric Utilities"), with charging moved to
"Ground infrastructure at utility substations", and offers a pilot slot. Price today: none public ([SITE], read
2026-10-22: no price or per-pole figure).

- **Any price amount.** Never published, at launch or since; the founder's $3 to $5 per pole is the operator's reading
  (item 7), and the header says so.
- **The cost per pole.** The founders give poles a day, not dollars; $4 to $10 is the author's arithmetic on [BLS].
- **Volumes.** How many poles a utility inspects a year is not asked by Keel (no volume question on `each`); the
  50,000-pole co-op is in the statement only.
- **A buyer title** and every Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment item beyond those quoted in item 5.
- **First-person lineman accounts.** None in the sources; the stories are scripted from the founders' post and the
  thread.
- **Which launch statement is "day one".** [LYC1] (2026-01-23) pitched power-line charging; the entry uses [HN]
  (2026-03-19), where that approach is dropped, as the idea the founders held at launch.

screens.why1: Once compatibility is settled, asking what the drone patrol does better than foot patrols is the natural next step in describing the solution.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain; 'the way they do it today' is obviously the lineman's foot patrol with binoculars and a checklist.
screens.why3: I know exactly why utilities switch: poles covered without trucks and walking, and the pole-top view that found 60% more defects for Xcel.
screens.why4: A free-text box with a single 'Leave this out of the study' escape is right for an advantage the founder must state, and the escape fits.
screens.why5: Keel's belief kept only the first of my two benefits and dropped 'defects on the pole tops seen up close', which is my strongest point; 'their last pole' also misreads a patrol of many poles as one pole.
screens.instead: Keep both benefits in the belief: For most, their last patrol would have gone better with it: every pole on the circuit checked without walking the line, and the pole tops seen up close from above.

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today's way, this lets me check Keel's list of benefits before it goes to linemen, so it is obvious why it is here.
screens.why2: Both rows are plain lineman's words ('walking the line', 'pole tops'), but the test line 'their last pole would have gone better' needs a second read: a lineman thinks in patrols or circuits, not one pole.
screens.why3: Any lineman who has patrolled a circuit with binoculars knows whether walking it and squinting up at the pole tops is the hard part, so both benefits are answerable from their own work.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in our words, but the speed benefit I sell on is missing: a circuit covered in a fraction of the time against 50-150 poles a day.
screens.why5: The benefits keep what I typed (coverage without foot patrols, and the pole-top vantage behind Xcel's 60% more defects), but the belief narrows my patrol to 'their last pole' and tests only the first row although the list says all are equal.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Every pole checked without walking the line' / 'Defects on the pole tops seen up close' / 'A whole circuit done in a day, not weeks'; test: 'For most, their last patrol would have gone better with it.'

screens.why1: After what it does better, asking what linemen must change to start using it is the natural next step, and it is the last of the four solution items, as the frame says.
screens.why2: "What will they have to do to start using it?" with a hint about setup, extra steps or learning is plain to me as a founder selling inspection as a service to utilities.
screens.why3: I know exactly what changes for a lineman: they stop walking circuits with binoculars and start checking the poles our drone flags, so I can answer it from my own work.
screens.why4: The only option is a box to type in plus the "Leave this out of the study" chip, and that escape fits a founder who would rather not test adoption.
screens.why5: Keel's belief keeps "review the poles a drone flags before sending crews" but drops my second half, "work from a defect list instead of patrolling," which is the bigger change to a lineman's day.

screens.why1: Right after I said what linemen would have to do to start, this is Keel handing back its draft of that friction, the last solution item before testing, so it plainly belongs here.
screens.why2: Flagged poles, sending crews and a defect list are how my linemen and their supervisors already talk, though the intro clumsily repeats the title word for word.
screens.why3: I know this from the pilot talks: the real change for a crew is trusting the drone's flags and rolling trucks off a list instead of walking every pole.
screens.why4: The two rows overlap, since reviewing the drone's flags and working from a defect list are one change seen twice. The first row is 9 words against an 'under 9' rule. A distinct step is missing: handing over circuit maps and pole locations.
screens.why5: It keeps what I typed: review the drone's flags before sending crews, work from a defect list, and the belief 'Most would' matches my read of the patrol.
screens.instead: What they'll have to do: 'Check drone-flagged poles before rolling a truck' / 'Patrol only the poles on the defect list' / 'Hand over circuit maps and pole locations'

screens.why1: Right after I named the efforts linemen must make to adopt it, asking which one is most likely to stop them is the obvious next step before the test is set.
screens.why2: Both options are in the words I'd use about my linemen, flagged poles, sending crews, defect list, patrolling, and the title reads cleanly on first pass.
screens.why3: I know from pilot talks that the open question is whether crews will trust and act on a drone's flags, so I can pick from what I know.
screens.why4: The two options overlap, since working from a defect list is mostly reviewing what the drone flagged, so the choice between them is thinner than it looks.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most would review the poles a drone flags before sending crews' is my adoption step word for word, and nothing about Voltair, pads or the buyer leaks into it.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? — Trust the poles a drone flags enough to send crews / Give up walking the circuit pole by pole

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, asking whether to collect pilot sign-ups is exactly where it belongs, and a pilot is how we sell ("If you're interested in piloting our service, reach out")
screens.why2: Offer a pilot, yes or no, with the exact line respondents will see quoted in the hint, is plain on first read
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads is my own call and I'm actively lining up pilots with utilities, so I answer it instantly
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and nothing is missing for a go/no-go switch
screens.why5: The meaning is kept, but "Would you try this for real?" will land on linemen, who can't commit a utility to a per-pole pilot; I'd want the ask to say whether it's a user trial or a buyer's paid pilot so I know who I'm actually collecting
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Respondents see: "Would you want your crew to try this on one of your circuits? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who reads my questions to linemen belongs right before the link goes out, after the pilot offer and before people see it.
screens.why2: It's clear to me, but "linemans" stops me on first read since nobody in the trade says that, and the hint says "voice" while the video interviewer also has a face, so I have to read it twice to know what 400 credits buys.
screens.why3: Picking which interviewer my crews will hear is my own call, and I can make it from two 5-second clips.
screens.why4: Two named voices, each with a listen button and a default already picked, is complete and distinct for this choice.
screens.why5: I typed "linemen who inspect poles at US power utilities", and Keel pluralised my role as "linemans", which is my word gone slightly wrong.
screens.instead: Who should ask linemen your questions? (Daphne ▶ hear her · Saskia ▶ hear her)

screens.why1: Choosing how the linemen answer belongs right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, so the reason for asking is obvious.
screens.why2: The options are plain, but 'linemens' is not a word; it trips me on first read, and the plural I typed was 'linemen'.
screens.why3: I know my linemen: they're in a truck or on a pole between jobs, so I can judge whether they'd rather talk to a video or read and tap.
screens.why4: AI voice, text and let-them-choose cover the real choices, are distinct, and each states plainly when it is ready.
screens.why5: The meaning is kept, but my 'linemen' has been respelled as the made-up plural 'linemens' (and 'linemans' on the screen before), which drifts from what I typed.
screens.instead: How should the linemen answer? — AI interviewer (Daphne) / Read and tap / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing how linemen answer, deciding who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices read plainly on first pass; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own term but explained by 'from a search'.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to linemen I've met at co-ops and utilities or posting in a group, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real cases, but the first option's label and description run together without punctuation ('People I know by name I send each one...'), and there's no mix option for when I have a few named linemen plus a forum post.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my study or leaks my product to respondents; it's purely about distribution.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (each gets their own link) / People I found with Keel (pick a Contacts list) / A group, with one open link (post it where linemen already are, e.g. a lineman forum or co-op newsletter)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside its deciding number on every card ('4 answered · 5 needed to call it'), so I know nothing is called and why: one more counted answer per card.
screens.why_b2: The stage page draws no chart, and the tally '3 too few · 7 people answered' takes a second look: is '3' the cards or the people, and why does 7 answered become 4 on each card?
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry exactly the belief lines I checked, word for word, though Keel's statement above them is garbled ('the lineman weatherized, long-range fixed-wing drones ... and gets back').
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next, such as sending the study to more linemen who were on patrol, or why 3 of my 7 were not counted.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing: n is visible everywhere and the low count is named as too few to call, though the 7-versus-4 gap is left unexplained.
screens.instead: Not called yet: 3 of your 7 weren't on a patrol this quarter, so only 4 count and you need 5. Send the study to one or two more linemen who walked poles recently to call all three.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits with "5 needed to call it" right under it, so I know why there's no answer and what number would settle it.
screens.why_b2: The chart shows four counted answers on the yes-to-no scale and my bar at 3 of 4, and the strip shows Dale as the fifth, uncounted cell.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "the pole tops could be seen from above" are word for word what I checked, though the question asked is the generic "would it have fitted" rather than about seeing pole tops.
screens.why_b4: It points me at Travis, whose line runs under thick timber with only treetops visible from the air, and that is exactly the canopy question I need to answer about my territory.
screens.why_b5: The verdict says "4 answered" while the count line says "5 answered · 4 counted", and "a lean, not a call" never says which way it leans (3 of 4 would clear my bar), so I have to piece it together.
screens.instead: Leaning held but too few to call: 3 of the 4 counted (5 answered, Dale's a guess) could see the pole tops, and one more counted answer would settle it. Ask Travis how much line runs under timber, because that is where the drone can't see.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside "4 answered · 5 needed to call it", so I know there's no verdict and exactly why.
screens.why_b2: Three better and one same over four counted is plain, but "your bar · 3 of 4" next to "no more than 1 in 3" takes a second look to see that 3 of 4 is the threshold and that I'm sitting on it, not past it.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and "every pole checked without walking the line" are word for word the belief I confirmed.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic; it doesn't tell me I'm one counted answer short, that Dale's guess is the gap, or that the lean so far meets my bar.
screens.why_b5: n is on the screen, Dale's exclusion is explained, the small group is called "a lean, not a call", and the question is flagged as hypothetical, so nothing claims more than four linemen can carry.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 linemen say a lot better, right at your bar of no more than 1 in 3 against; one more counted answer decides it, so get Dale or another lineman to name an actual last patrol.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the deciding number, 4 counted against the 5 needed, so I know where it stands and why.
screens.why_b2: The bars (1 yes, 2 yes-if-worth-it, 1 probably not) over 4 people read at once, but the bar mixes '3 of 4' with 'no more than 1 in 3', and Dale's ghost cell made me look twice to see whether my 3 of 4 clears it.
screens.why_b3: 'Adoption friction' and 'Most would review the poles a drone flags before sending crews' are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me to get one more lineman's answer, or that two of my three yeses hang on the drone's flags being clearly worth the review.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said plainly ('a small group: a lean, not a call', '2 on a condition'), but the verdict line says '4 answered' while the count line says 5 answered and 4 counted, a small contradiction about who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 5 linemen counted (Dale's was a guess), 3 would review the flags, but 2 only if the flags are clearly worth it; one more clear answer calls it, so show them a sample flagged-pole list.

screens.why_b1: Each box says "Too few to call" with "4 answered · 5 needed to call it" right under it, so the verdict and the number that decides it sit together.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Relative advantage carry the exact belief lines I checked on the way in, pole tops seen from above and every pole checked without walking the line.
screens.why_b4: "5 needed to call it" hints that I should get more linemen to answer, but nothing says what a canopy-blocked line or a patrol that already works means for where I fly first or how I pitch, and Adoption friction is missing with no word on why.
screens.why_b5: The low n is stated on every box, each quote is labelled as one person on their own, and nothing is called a pattern.
screens.why_b6: Lines under thick timber where a top-down view sees treetops, and a lineman whose week is run by trouble calls and a short crew rather than patrols, are both limits I did not write into my idea.
screens.instead: Too few to call (4 of 5): ask one more lineman; the one no on each line is a real limit to probe: timber-covered lines block the top-down view, and for some crews the pain is trouble calls and short staffing, not the patrol itself. Adoption friction: no one against.

screens.why1: A first screen that asks whether I've walked poles lately makes sense before anything else, since that's the whole subject.
screens.why2: I'd answer it fine, but nobody I work with says they 'tried to check poles one by one'; we'd say we did a ground patrol or ground-line inspection, and the 'try to' makes it sound like I might have failed at it.
screens.why3: Walking a circuit and checking each pole from the ground with the clipboard and binoculars is exactly what I've been doing these last three months.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the chips don't belong: a yes-or-no gate shouldn't carry an escape at all, 'I can't recall one particular pole' doesn't answer whether I did the work, and 'I'd rather not say' is one the rules say doesn't exist.
screens.why5: Nothing of anybody's product reaches me, but the founder's 'have to be checked one by one' turned into 'did you try to check', which drifts from doing the job to attempting it.
screens.why6: Said aloud it's one short question and 'Yes or no,' easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you inspect poles on a circuit from the ground, pole by pole? Yes / No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: After asking whether I checked poles one by one from the ground, showing me an idea for inspecting them another way is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Pole, span, feeder, thermal and storm patrol are my words, but LiDAR, fixed-wing and 'weatherized' are drone-vendor talk, not lineman talk, and I'd need a second read to picture what the pads are.
screens.why3: It's about the poles and spans I walk and the post-storm patrols I do, so I can judge it from my own work.
screens.why4: A card to read, no options shown.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose and comes through clear, but 'rapid scan' and the pitch-like 'only cheap charging pads' read like the founder's sales line rather than plain description.
screens.why6: It's a long block said in one go, and 'LiDAR', the colon-list 'high-resolution photos, LiDAR and thermal' and 'fixed-wing' are a mouthful to hear once on a phone.
screens.instead: Imagine Voltair, drones that photograph every pole for you. They live out on the line for months, charging on small pads, and fly pole to pole taking close-up and heat photos. You can send them out right after a storm or when a circuit acts up. The people building it believe it would only need cheap charging pads along the lines.

screens.why1: Right after the drone-photo idea, asking whether it would have worked on the last pole I checked makes sense.
screens.why2: "Fitted the way things were set up for you" is fuzzy: I can't tell if it means our crew's routine, the company's rules on flying drones, or whether you could even get a drone up at that pole, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I know my last pole, under trees, along a road, in a backyard easement, but whether drone shots would fit how we're set up depends on the company's drone rules and who'd fly it, so I'd be half guessing.
screens.why4: "Yes, most of the time" and "Only sometimes" don't fit one pole: that pole either would have worked or it wouldn't.
screens.why5: The card says plainly what it is, but the question lost what has to fit, so it drifts into a general "would it suit you".
screens.why6: Short, one question, and four short options plus one escape are easy to hold when heard.
screens.instead: Think of your last pole. Could a drone have got clear photos of it where it stood? I'll read three options. Yes; yes, with some steps; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after I've been told about Voltair and asked if it would fit how we're set up, it makes sense to ask whether it would have actually helped on the last pole I checked.
screens.why2: I'd answer it, but 'made your last pole go better' reads funny, since a pole doesn't go anywhere; it's the inspection of it that goes better or worse, so I'd have to read it twice.
screens.why3: I just walked a circuit and checked poles from the ground, so I know whether drone shots would have shown me more than my binoculars did on that one.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference or worse covers it with no overlap, and 'I can't tell' fits if I've never seen what a drone picture of a cross-arm or a cotter pin looks like.
screens.why5: It's still drone photos of every pole held up against the pole I checked from the ground, and nothing about the company's plans or their own words for me leaks through beyond the card itself.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options I can hold in my head, and the escape is said last.
screens.instead: Would Voltair have made checking your last pole go better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether it would fit and whether it would help, it makes sense to ask whether I'd take on the extra step it needs.
screens.why2: Reviewing flagged poles and sending crews is how we talk on the job, so I get it the first time I hear it.
screens.why3: I do look over poles that get written up, but sending crews is usually my supervisor's or the engineer's call, so I'd be partly guessing about that half.
screens.why4: The four answers run cleanly from yes to no, and the one with a condition is what most of us would actually say, with 'I can't tell' fitting as the way out.
screens.why5: It still sounds like the drone idea, but 'before sending crews' quietly makes me the one who dispatches, and that drifts a little from a lineman checking poles.
screens.why6: It's one short question and four short answers I can hold in my head after hearing them once.
